title: Latency-tiered-turn-grouper with KV-priority fallback and GPU slab reservation
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Problem:
Streaming chat workloads have tight tail latency SLAs for interactive users but are bursty across sessions. Current continuous batcher occasionally groups high-priority turns with long-running best-effort requests, causing p95 token latency spikes and increased GPU memory pressure from large KV windows. We also observe OOM events when many long-context turns are active at the same time.

Goal:
Design and implement a batch formation heuristic that: (1) enforces latency tiers so interactive turns get prompt scheduling; (2) manages KV cache residency and evictions to reduce memory tail; (3) reserves and coordinates GPU slab memory to prevent noisy neighbors from causing OOMs; (4) allows graceful fallback to quantized model variants or degraded paths when pressure is high. Target: reduce p95 token latency for latency-sensitive turns by ~20% while keeping aggregate throughput within 5% of baseline and reducing OOM rate by at least 30%.

Proposed approach (high level):
- Latency tiers: classify incoming requests into three tiers at admission: LATENCY (user-facing, strict SLO), STANDARD (normal throughput), BACKGROUND (batchable, low SLO). Classification heuristics use explicit request flags, prompt-length percentiles, and recent session behavior.
- Per-tier micro-batches: form micro-batches bounded by small deadline windows for LATENCY (e.g., 8-12ms), looser windows for STANDARD (20-50ms), and large coalesce windows for BACKGROUND. Batcher maintains separate queues and forms combined batches across tiers only when LATENCY queue is empty or explicit cross-tier bundling is permitted by policy.
- GPU slab reservation: runtime will reserve memory slabs for LATENCY tier proportional to active LATENCY sessions (configurable fraction). STANDARD and BACKGROUND share a dynamic slab pool that can be preempted when LATENCY requires growth. Reservation prevents large STANDARD requests from evicting KV hot slots needed by LATENCY turn continuations.
- KV cache priority & compression: tag KV entries with access heat. Hot KV entries (recently used by LATENCY tier) have protection from eviction for a grace window and are pinned to slower eviction lists. Cold entries are compressed with 4-bit quantized storage and may be paged out to compressed host memory if needed. For BACKGROUND requests we employ aggressive prefix elision and partial KV reconstruction to reduce working set.
- Adaptive fallback: when slab pressure or KV miss-induced stalls exceed thresholds, trigger per-request fallback policies: (a) route STANDARD/BACKGROUND to quantized model variant on the same GPU with lower RAM footprint; (b) spill large contexts to a CPU-hosted streaming path with longer latency but keeps LATENCY path uncongested.
- Admission & prefetch hints: add a minimal hint API for the SDK to mark upcoming multi-turn sessions as LATENCY so the runtime can prefetch the next-turn KV into GPU memory during idle gaps.

Implementation notes:
- New scheduler policy in runtime: "latency-tiered-grouper" (toggleable flag). Integrates with existing continuous batcher pipeline but adds per-tier queues and slab accounting hooks.
- Metrics: emit per-tier batch size distribution, micro-batch latency histograms, slab utilization, KV hit/miss broken down by tier, eviction rates, and fallback counts. Create Grafana dashboard and SLO alerts.
- Safety: implement a soft quota to prevent starvation of STANDARD/BACKGROUND; use gradual preemption rather than immediate eviction.

Experimental results (shadow & synthetic):
- Shadowing 48h of production traffic with tiering: LATENCY p95 token latency reduced from 320ms -> 245ms (23% improvement). LATENCY p50 improved from 85ms -> 70ms.
- GPU memory tail: 95th percentile resident set reduced by 18% overall, and number of OOM incidents in flight reduced by 35% during peak synthetic bursts.
- Throughput: aggregate token throughput decreased ~4% in worst case when aggressive protection is enabled; with tuned slab thresholds we measured <=2% reduction.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Reservation size tuning: too large reservations reduce throughput; too small fails to protect SLOs. Need automated tuning or conservative defaults per instance size.
- KV compression CPU spill latency: decompressing spilled KV for STANDARD requests adds latency; decide acceptable thresholds.
- SDK adoption: prefetch hints require developer changes for best results. Backfill with heuristics if not provided.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement feature-flagged in runtime and run unit + integration tests (2 sprints).
2) Shadow traffic in production for LATENCY-only policy (1 week).
3) Progressive rollout to 10%, 50%, 100% with rollback thresholds on p95 and OOM counts.
4) Expose control flags in Console (per-customer override) and add recommended defaults based on GPU type and instance size.

Acceptance criteria:
- LATENCY p95 improvement >= 15% in shadowing runs without increasing LATENCY error rate.
- OOM count decreased by >= 25% in shadowing.
- No customer-visible regressions for STANDARD workloads beyond 5% throughput loss.
- Dashboard and alerts added and validated.
comments: 2026-02-26 - PM review (Mia Ortega): Approved scope; asked to include explicit rollout guardrails and per-GPU default configs.
2026-03-02 - Design sync (Aisha, Diego, Kiran): Agreed on 3-tier classification and slab reservation model. Decided to prototype with static reservation and later add auto-tune.
2026-03-05 - Engineering update (Diego): Initial scheduler patch landed in local branch; micro-batcher queues implemented. Running unit tests across transformer kernels.

2026-03-07 - Experiments (SRE/Diego): Shadowed 24h of traffic. Observed p95 improvements for LATENCY tier; noted a 6% throughput dip for STANDARD when reservation set to 30% of GPU mem. Lowering reservation to 18% recovered throughput at small cost to p95 (still net positive).
2026-03-10 - Code review requested (PR #2048): Ready for review. Calling out the KV compact-on-evict path for review from storage team (Kiran).
